lines.text: A diamond is the hourglass turned inside out. That isn't a joke — it's the whole trick.
With the hourglass you asked: how far am I from the nearest edge?
With a diamond you ask the opposite question: how far am I from the middle?
Let's do it by hand first, before any code. Five rows, so the middle one is row two. Watch two numbers as we go down.
Row zero. You're two steps from the middle — so, two spaces, then one star.
Row one. One step away. One space, three stars.
Row two. You're on it. No spaces at all, five stars.
Row three. One step again, the other way. One space, three stars.
Row four. Two steps. Two spaces, one star.
Now read the spaces column straight down the page. Two, one, zero, one, two. It goes in, and it comes back out.
That's the diamond. You've just drawn it with numbers, and you haven't written a line of code.
So there's your rule. The spaces are how far you are from the middle. And the stars are whatever's left of the row once you've taken those spaces off both sides — five, minus two lots of the gap.
The line doing the real work is the one with the distance in it. That abs just means how far, ignoring which side you're on — two steps above the middle and two steps below are both simply two.
And now the nice bit. Change that one question back to how far from the edge, and you've got the hourglass again. Same loops. Same printing. One different question.
That's usually what separates two shapes. Not the code. The question.
